title: Retiring, still serving
hookLine: leaving paid work and continuing to serve
tomorrow: the wedding budget fight. can three old words settle it?

lines: A LAST SHIFT, AND A HANDED-OVER KEY.
cards: Diesel, burnt coffee, and the hiss of air brakes. That's what the yard smells and sounds like at six in the morning, and Chacha Balwinder, Jasleen's dad, has known it longer than Simran has been alive.
Today is his last shift driving for Harjit's company. The drivers clap him out of the yard. Somebody honks a horn too long.
Then, in the parking lot, he hands Harjit his keys and says the thing nobody expects. Tomorrow at six he'll be somewhere else. Where?

teach.b: The answer has a different smell: onions in hot oil, cardamom tea, and the clatter of stacked steel trays. Chacha's new six a.m. is the gurdwara langar kitchen. Sikhi has no word for stopping serving.
Paid work can end. Seva, selfless service, doesn't retire.

On ang 26, Guru Nanak says, in paraphrase, serve in this world, and you will be given a seat in the Lord's court. Service isn't a phase of life; it's the shape of it. And here's one to tell a friend tonight.
Tradition says Guru Amar Das came to Guru Angad late in life, an old man by then, and served him anyway, carrying water before dawn, in heat and rain. The one who served became the third Guru.
So the tradition doesn't picture old age as sitting still.
It pictures hands that keep moving, at a gentler pace. Not everyone can stand at a tava for hours, and seva doesn't ask that.
It can be folding chairs, sitting with the sick, teaching a grandchild Gurmukhi, reading Gurbani to someone whose eyes have dimmed. Chacha's hands, which held a wheel for years, now hold a ladle.
He says the dal is harder to steer.

how: Some older Sikhs give time to seva after leaving paid work: cooking or cleaning in langar, caring for the gurdwara, teaching children or reading Gurbani with others.

o: handing your savings to the community at old age
leaving paid work while keeping up selfless service
stepping back from the gurdwara to rest at home

games.q: the last shift and the next one — tap the pairs.
p: served late in life, carrying water

s: in Sikhi, retirement is the time to finally stop serving
paid work can end; seva, selfless service, doesn't retire.
tradition says Guru Amar Das came to Guru Angad late in life and served him
carrying water before dawn; he became the third Guru.
seva only counts if it's heavy work in the kitchen
folding chairs, sitting with the sick, reading Gurbani to someone: all seva.

games.q: your grandfather retires and says he's too old to be useful at the gurdwara now. his knees are bad. what does today's lesson offer him?
o: seva fits the body: reading Gurbani to someone, or teaching a grandchild.
he's earned his rest; seva is really for the young.
he should push through and stand in the kitchen anyway.
games.why: seva doesn't retire, but it changes pace. the tradition pictures hands that keep moving, gently, the way Guru Amar Das served late in life.

practice: Rest your hands on your knees, palms up, and look at them for a while: the lines, the knuckles, any scars or calluses they've picked up. Think of a few things they've carried for other people over the years.
Then close them gently and keep that weight in mind as you sit, and one thing these hands might still carry for someone, years from now.

wordCard.voice: Retiring. Leaving paid work, and in Sikhi, carrying on with seva at whatever pace the body allows.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: seva, selfless service, the work that doesn't retire.

carryVoice: Keep serving: the paycheck stops, the seva doesn't, and Chacha starts at six tomorrow, ladle in hand. Day done.
